summary: Gives a framework and service-level requirements for Layer 1 Virtual Private Networks, where a provider offers customers private connectivity over its lower-level transport network. It covers why such services are wanted, what they must provide, and some architectural models for building them. It is informational and guides later protocol work.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine a phone company renting you a private wire that only you can use, even though the cables are shared with others. This note describes what that rental should look like and how it could be built.

questions: how do providers share layer 1 networks
subtitle: Allowing service providers to offer virtual private networks at the optical and circuit-switched layer.

tldr.problem: Service providers want to offer customers dedicated connectivity at the lowest network layer (Layer 1), like renting a private circuit, but need a framework for how to build these services dynamically and support multiple customers on shared infrastructure.
tldr.mechanism: L1VPNs extend VPN concepts to Layer 1 by defining service models where providers use GMPLS (a routing and switching control protocol) to manage customer connections. Different models provide varying levels of control and routing visibility to customers.
tldr.outcome: This framework enables providers to offer both static private lines and dynamic on-demand Layer 1 services, allowing customers to share expensive fiber and optical networks while maintaining service isolation.

today: RFC 4847 is an Informational RFC that establishes the framework for L1VPN services. While it has not been made obsolete, it was succeeded in some areas by additional RFCs that define specific protocols and mechanisms for L1VPN deployment. The framework remains relevant for providers designing VPN services at the optical and circuit layer.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 4847 establishes a framework for Layer 1 Virtual Private Networks (L1VPNs), a service where a network provider offers layer 1 connectivity to customers between multiple sites. The RFC examines why customers want these services, what they require, and architectural models for building them.

L1VPNs operate at the optical or circuit-switched layer (Time Division Multiplexing switches, optical cross-connects) rather than the data link or IP layer. They are controlled using GMPLS, a protocol suite that brings standardized, scalable control to layer 1 networks. The framework is designed to guide development of protocols and mechanisms for interoperable L1VPN services.
sections.plainLanguage: At the lowest level of the network are light paths and time slots that carry signals. An L1VPN lets a customer rent some of these paths so they connect only their offices together.

sections.title: Motivations and Benefits
sections.content:
Customers benefit from L1VPNs in two main ways. First, they can outsource management of layer 1 infrastructure to the provider, freeing themselves from configuring and managing connectivity between their edge devices. Second, they can use layer 1 networks at small scale by sharing infrastructure with other customers, avoiding the expense of deploying and managing their own network.

Providers benefit by building on-demand services and extracting more value from their network resources. Instead of requiring customers to configure end-to-end connections, the provider takes on that responsibility. Providers can also use unused capacity more flexibly by applying models where resources are allocated dynamically.

Multiple deployment scenarios exist: a multi-service backbone where one organization's departments share a layer 1 network; a carrier's carrier where one service provider is a customer of another; layer 1 resource trading where a provider sources services from multiple upstream providers; and scheduling services where customers reserve bandwidth at planned times in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone company saves money by renting out pieces of the same wire to many customers instead of building separate wires. Customers save money by not having to build and maintain their own network.

sections.title: Network Architecture and Devices
sections.content:
The L1VPN architecture consists of three kinds of devices. CE (Customer Edge) devices belong to the customer and connect the customer's network to the provider. A CE can be a TDM switch, an optical cross-connect (OXC), or a more general device like a router that is connected to layer 1 infrastructure. PE (Provider Edge) devices belong to the provider and offer the L1VPN service to customers; they are connected to CEs. P (Provider) devices form the core of the provider network, connected only to other P and PE devices.

Layer 1 connections are provided between pairs of CEs within the same VPN. These connections may follow a hierarchy: for instance, a VC3 time slot could be carried within an STM1 (SONET) connection. The provider's management system handles provisioning, monitoring, and billing. Customer management systems may communicate with provider systems to request connections and obtain information.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of CE as the customer's connection box, PE as the provider's box at the edge of their network, and P as the provider's internal network. Layer 1 connections are the actual light paths or time slots that carry data between customers.

sections.title: Service Models
sections.content:
The RFC describes three main service models that differ in how much information the provider shares with the customer. The Management-Based Service Model involves only management-plane communication: a customer management system talks to a provider management system to request connections. There is no direct control plane exchange between CE and PE.

The Signaling-Based Service Model (Overlay) allows CE-PE signaling for path setup only. The customer requests a connection to a specific remote CE using GMPLS signaling, but receives no routing information about the provider network or other customer sites. The provider's membership information (which CEs can connect to which) must be configured on the PE.

The Signaling and Routing Service Model (Enhanced) adds limited routing and traffic engineering information exchange. The CE can learn about remote customer sites and the dedicated resources available to it, allowing customers to perform traffic engineering like creating disjoint paths between sites. Four variants exist: Overlay Extension, Virtual Node, Virtual Link, and Per-VPN Peer models, each providing different levels of visibility into the provider network.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways to ask the phone company for a connection: send a request to their office, tell the edge device at your location where you want to go, or learn some information about the network and plan your own route.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
Several real-world deployment scenarios motivate L1VPN design. In a Multi-Service Backbone, a single carrier's different service departments (e.g., IP services, ATM services) are customers of a shared layer 1 transport network. Each department gets its own independent address space, fault isolation, and resource view, while the provider network itself is service-agnostic.

A Carrier's Carrier scenario involves one service provider as a customer of another. The upstream provider gives the downstream provider limited visibility and control, allowing each to focus on its own layer of service. Layer 1 Resource Trading occurs when a provider sources services from multiple upstream providers and can choose routes and providers dynamically based on price or availability. An enterprise can also use an L1VPN to increase reliability by receiving services from multiple providers.

Inter-AS and Inter-SP L1VPNs support connections that span multiple administrative domains within a provider or across multiple providers, though these require further analysis. Scheduling Services allow customers to reserve connections at a future time or tolerate setup delays, enabling more efficient bandwidth utilization for backup and content delivery applications.
sections.plainLanguage: Different companies use L1VPNs in different ways: a bank might use one to connect its offices, a phone company might buy connections from a bigger phone company, or a disaster recovery service might book connections in advance for off-peak times.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC identifies that L1VPNs involve multiple types of security-sensitive information: customer topology and addressing information, provider network topology and resource information, and control messages between entities. Different service models expose different amounts of information, which has security implications.

In management-based models, information exchanges happen through management channels, which may be protected by existing management security mechanisms. Signaling-based models rely on GMPLS security at the CE-PE interface. Enhanced models with routing exchange require careful control of what routing information is shared between the customer and provider, and among different customers. Customers may benefit from using mechanisms such as address translation at their interfaces to protect their addressing realms from exposure to the provider network.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone company needs to keep each customer's data secret from other customers, and each customer should not be able to see or interfere with the company's network or other customers' wires.
